newsitem.title: UK: Indian stowaway fights British deportation.
newsitem.headline: Indian stowaway fights British deportation.

text.p: Politicians and refugee groups are urging a British minister to intervene in the case of an Indian man who is facing deportation after he stowed away in the wheel carriage of a British Airways jumbo jet on a flight from New Delhi.

Pardeep Saini, 22, will appeal to the Home Office (interior ministry) on Friday after it refused his bid for political asylum. His supporters said Home Secretary Michael Howard should use his influence because of the extraordinary circumstances of the case.
Doctors said it is nothing short of a miracle that Saini survived the 10-hour trip from India to Britain in temperatures of -60C (-76F) in the wheel storage compartment of the Boeing 747.
His younger brother Vijay, 19, froze to death and his body was dumped as the jet's wheels were lowered on approach to London's Heathrow Airport last October.

"This is obviously an exceptional case where someone has undergone incredible personal suffering and lost a brother as well," Conservative MP Jim Lester, chairman of the all-party parliamentary refugee group, told a British newspaper.

"Whatever the simple legal interpretation, it should be reviewed by a minister because here are special circumstances which require a real understanding of the human dimensions of this case," he added.

Claude Moraes, director of the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants, warned that high risk illegal immigration was on the rise because genuine asylum seekers were finding the doors to some European Union countries tightly shut.
"We want the government to take into account the dangerous circumstances of the case and to show compassion," he told Reuters.

Saini and his brother fled Punjab after being accused of being supporters of Sikh separatists, which they deny. They were promised safe passage to Britain by agents in New Delhi who claimed the wheel storage of the jet led to the baggage hold. It didn't.
The brothers climbed into the undercarriage and the jet took off almost immediately.

Doctors said Saini probably lost consciousness and went into a state of suspended animation which helped to prevent brain damage. Saini has said he does not remember anything that happened during the flight or the landing.
"He's lucky to be alive," an immigration official said after he found Saini wandering around a runway at Heathrow airport last October. Saini was taken to hospital for treatment for hypothermia.
